By transforming large-scale and complex clinical datasets into interpretable visual formats, such as imaging overlays, predictive dashboards, and interactive diagnostic charts, these systems improve the accuracy, speed, and reliability of clinical decision-making. Integrating machine learning and data visualization techniques, AI enables healthcare professionals to identify patterns, detect anomalies, and assess patient risks more effectively across diverse medical domains, including radiology, cardiology, and chronic disease management. Despite these advantages, challenges such as data privacy concerns, model interpretability limitations, algorithmic bias, and integration difficulties with existing healthcare infrastructure continue to hinder widespread adoption. This paper examines the role of AI-driven visualization in strengthening Clinical Decision Support Systems, highlighting its contributions to diagnostic improvement, workflow optimization, and patient care enhancement, while also addressing its ethical, technical, and operational constraints.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.6928898\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.1016/j.dss.2024.114193\", \"title\": [\"Navigating autonomy and control in human-AI delegation: User responses to technology- versus user-invoked task allocation\"], \"URL…

Transformer-based architectures enable models capable of reasoning, summarization, and natural language interaction across a wide range of domains. Despite these advances, most deployed systems remain fundamentally stateless. Interactions are typically constrained by bounded context windows and lack persistent understanding of individual users. This limitation restricts the development of truly personal artificial intelligence systems capable of long-term interaction, adaptation, and cognitive support. Human cognition develops across time through accumulated experiences and reflection. Artificial intelligence systems that cannot store and interpret long-term memory remain limited in their ability to support these processes. This paper proposes a conceptual framework for persistent memory in personal artificial intelligence systems. We introduce a layered memory architecture consisting of conversational memory, semantic memory, and reflective memory. These memory layers enable artificial intelligence systems to maintain evolving representations of individuals and support long-term interaction. Persistent memory architectures may therefore represent a foundational component of next-generation personal artificial intelligence systems designed to augment human reflection, decision-making, and cognitive processes.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.6349019\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.7551/mitpress/10591.003.0005\", \"title\": [\"Situating Episodic Memory\"], \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.7551/mitpress/10591.003.0005\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2016, 2, 5]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.54941/ahfe1004643\", \"title\": [\"Episodic Memory with Interactive 3D Sequential Graph\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>Episodic…
